Only 1 Dollar in 10 Is Cash. How Banks Create Money Out of Thin Air

2026-11-13

Subscribe for one money story a week

About this video

Only about 1 dollar in 10 in America is physical cash: $2.5 trillion of currency out of $23.4 trillion in M2 (September 2026). Most of the rest was created by banks when they made loans. A loan doesn't lend out someone else's savings: it creates a brand-new deposit, and paying the loan back destroys that money. The Bank of England explained this in 2014. We follow a $300,000 mortgage through a bank's books, show where cash fits in, why the US reserve requirement has been 0% since March 2020, what really limits banks (borrowers, capital, interest rates and confidence), what happened at Silicon Valley Bank, and how the 2020 money flood (M2 up about 40%, the Fed's balance sheet from $4.2 trillion to almost $9 trillion) came before 9% inflation. 0:00 Intro: 1 dollar in 10 0:27 The textbook story 0:59 How a loan creates money 1:47 Paying it back destroys money 2:44 Where cash fits in 3:08 How much money is there? 4:01 What stops banks? 5:06 When the promise breaks 5:45 The Fed and the 2020 money flood 7:16 What it means for you 7:52 Recap Sources: Bank of England, "Money creation in the modern economy", Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1 (McLeay, Radia and Thomas). FDIC: deposit insurance up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. Transcript

Only about one dollar in ten in America is actual cash. The other nine? They were typed into existence by banks, when they made loans. That's not a conspiracy theory. The Bank of England said it in 2014. And once you see how it works, you'll never look at your bank balance the same way. In the next ten minutes: how a loan creates money, how paying it back destroys it, what stops banks from creating infinite money, and what it all means for you. Most of us learned a simple story. You put a hundred dollars in the bank. The bank keeps a little and lends the rest to someone else. In the textbook version, called the money multiplier, the bank keeps ten percent and lends out ninety. That ninety lands in another bank, which lends out eighty-one, and so on. It sounds neat. But in 2014, the Bank of England published a paper called Money creation in the modern economy, and it says that isn't how banks work in practice. Banks don't wait for your deposit to make a loan. The loan makes the deposit. Let's watch it happen. Meet Maya. She wants to buy a house, and asks her bank for a 300,000 dollar mortgage. The bank checks her income and her credit. Then it says yes. Now here's the trick. The bank doesn't open a vault and hand her someone else's savings. It types 300,000 dollars into Maya's account. On the bank's books, two lines appear. Something it owns: Maya owes the bank 300,000 dollars. And something it owes: the bank owes Maya 300,000 dollars. That's her new deposit. The two lines balance. And 300,000 dollars of brand-new money now exists that didn't exist a minute ago. Maya pays the seller. The money moves from her bank to the seller's bank, but it doesn't disappear. It's now part of the money supply: money that you and I could end up holding. And here's the part almost nobody knows. When Maya repays her loan, that money is destroyed. Each payment cancels part of both lines. Her debt shrinks, and the deposit she paid with is gone. The interest is different. That's the bank's income. It pays salaries, it pays savers, and the rest is profit. And that interest adds up. In late October, the average 30-year mortgage rate was about 7.3 percent. At that rate, Maya's 300,000 dollar loan costs about 2,061 dollars a month. Over thirty years, she pays back about 742 thousand dollars, and about 442 thousand of that is interest. Meanwhile, the average savings account pays about 0.38 percent a year. That gap, between what banks charge borrowers and what they pay savers, is a big part of how banks make money. So money is always being born and destroyed. New loans create it. Repayments erase it. So where does physical cash come in? In the US, paper money is printed by the Treasury, and the Federal Reserve hands it out to banks. But cash only reaches you when you take it out of your account. Withdraw a hundred dollars from an ATM, and your bank balance drops by a hundred. No new money was created. It just changed form: from a number on a screen to paper in your hand. So how much money is out there? In the US, the broad measure is called M2: cash, plus checking and savings accounts, plus a few similar accounts. In September 2026, M2 was about 23.4 trillion dollars. Physical cash in circulation? About 2.5 trillion. That's the one dollar in ten. In 1960, M2 was about 304 billion dollars. Today, it's more than seventy times bigger. The economy and prices grew a lot over those decades too. But most of that money was created the same way Maya's was: by banks making loans. Right now, US commercial banks hold about 19.8 trillion dollars of deposits, and about 14.2 trillion dollars of loans. Most of the rest of what they own is government bonds, other securities, and reserves at the Fed. So if banks can type money into existence, why don't they create infinite amounts? You might think it's the reserve requirement: the rule that banks must keep a slice of their deposits at the central bank. In the US, that requirement has been zero since March 2020. Banks still hold about 3 trillion dollars of reserves anyway, because they need cash on hand to pay each other and their customers. So the requirement isn't what holds them back. The real limits are different. Limit one: borrowers. A bank needs people it trusts to pay it back. When a borrower can't pay, the bank takes the loss. Limit two: capital. Regulators make banks fund part of their loans with their own money, the shareholders' money, as a cushion against losses. Limit three: interest rates. The Federal Reserve sets the rate that ripples through every loan. When rates go up, borrowing gets expensive, fewer people borrow, and less new money gets created. And limit four: confidence. Your deposit is a promise. If too many people want that promise paid at once, a bank can run out of cash. That's exactly what happened to Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023. The bank had put a lot of its customers' money into long-term bonds. When interest rates jumped, those bonds lost value, and when customers heard, they rushed to get their money out. On March 9, customers tried to pull out 42 billion dollars in a single day, according to the Federal Reserve's own review. The next day, the bank was shut down. That's why the US has deposit insurance. The FDIC covers up to 250,000 dollars per depositor, per bank, for each type of account ownership. Most people's money sits well under that limit. But it's worth knowing the rule. So where does the Federal Reserve come in? The Fed creates a different kind of money: reserves, the money banks use to pay each other. It mostly does this by buying government bonds and mortgage bonds, and paying for them with brand-new reserves. That's called quantitative easing. In March 2020, as the pandemic hit, the Fed's balance sheet was about 4.2 trillion dollars. By April 2022, it had more than doubled, to almost 9 trillion. At the same time, the government sent out stimulus, banks kept lending, and deposits poured in. From February 2020 to March 2022, M2 jumped about 41 percent, from 15.5 to 21.8 trillion dollars. In February 2021, it was growing almost 27 percent a year: the fastest pace in data going back to 1960. And what came next? Inflation hit about 9 percent in June 2022, the highest in about four decades. Economists still argue about how much of that was the money, and how much was supply chains and energy. But the timing is hard to ignore. Since then, the Fed has shrunk its balance sheet to about 6.7 trillion dollars, and M2 is about 23.4 trillion. And something rare happened as interest rates rose. From December 2022 to early 2024, M2 was smaller than a year before: the first yearly drops in data going back to 1960. Fewer new loans, more repayments, so money was destroyed faster than it was created. And inflation today is about 4 percent. So what does all this mean for you? Three things. This isn't financial advice, just how the system works. One: the money in your bank account is a promise from your bank, insured up to 250,000 dollars. That's why the limit matters. Two: when you borrow, you're not borrowing someone else's savings. You're creating new money, and the interest you pay is how the bank earns from it. Three: when new money is created faster than the economy grows, prices can rise, and cash sitting still slowly loses value. Our inflation video shows exactly how much. Let's recap. Only about one dollar in ten is cash. Banks create most money by making loans, and repayments destroy it. The reserve requirement is zero, so what really limits banks is borrowers, capital, interest rates, and trust. So here's my question: did you know banks create money when they lend?
